previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a man with a history of coronary artery disease, diabetes, hypertension, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions, was admitted for worsening shortness of breath, chest pressure on exertion, leg swelling, and recent weight gain. He denied typical anginal pain, and serial EKGs and cardiac enzymes were unchanged and negative, ruling out acute coronary syndrome. Chest imaging showed signs of fluid overload and chronic bronchiectasis. He was diagnosed with acute on chronic diastolic heart failure and treated with intravenous furosemide and the addition of spironolactone. His symptoms improved, and he was discharged home in stable condition on optimized medical therapy, including continued antiplatelet, beta-blocker, and statin treatment. He was advised on fluid and salt restriction, daily weight monitoring, and outpatient follow-up with lab testing for electrolyte monitoring.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ y/o ___ only speaking male with hx CAD s/p multiple 
PCI, dCHF presenting with progressive shortness of breath and 
chest pressure. 

Chest pain: He had a known history of CAD with multiple PCI 
presenting a concern for MI. The patient endorsed chest pressure 
on arrival to the floor, however this resolved on its own 
without sublingual nitrogen. CXR did not reveal any acute 
cardiopulmonary process and his EKG was unchanged from prior 
with a troponin level of <0.01. He remained chest pain free for 
the remainder of his hospitalization.

SOB: In the emergency room, the patient endorsed worsening of 
his chest pressure with deep breathing. A chest x-ray was 
unrevealing, and a d-dimer was negative making pulmonary 
embolism unlikely, and a BNP of 7 was measured making a CHF 
exacerbation unlikely. On arrival to the floor he was able to 
breath comfortably when his chest pressure resolved. He 
experienced subjective shortness of breath with ambulation 
however his 02 sat's remained at 100% on ambulation. 

Orthostasis: The patient stated lightheadedness on sitting up on 
his first hospital day, and he was found to be orthostatic. His 
lasix was held during his hospitalization and his spironolactone 
was continued. On discharge, his spironolactone was discontinued 
and his lasix was restarted. 

Renal Insufficiency: On admission his creatinine was found to be 
1.5, elevated from a baseline of 1.0. He had recently been 
started on spironolactone as an outpatient. Initially his lasix, 
valsartan and spironolactone were held. He received gentle 
hydration with resolution of his renal failure and his 
spironolactone was restarted. 

Diabetes: During his hospitalization his glucose was well 
controlled on a regular insulin sliding scale, and his metformin 
and actos were held, with resumption on discharge.
